questions.question: How do you do back-of-the-envelope estimation for system design? What numbers should you know?
questions.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation: Capacity Planning for System Design
questions.direct_answer: Estimate by **breaking the system into 4 dimensions** — **traffic (QPS), storage, bandwidth, memory** — starting from a few user-level inputs (DAU, actions per user, data per action). Memorize **latency numbers** (L1 ~1ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD ~100μs, network round-trip ~1ms in-region / ~100ms cross-continent), **storage units** (1KB tweet, 100KB image, 1MB doc, 10MB video minute), and **scale anchors** (1 server ~10K QPS, Redis ~100K ops/sec, Kafka partition ~10MB/sec). The goal isn't precision — it's **order-of-magnitude correctness** so you can pick the right architecture (single DB vs sharded, in-memory vs disk, single region vs global).

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with key numbers, ability to derive QPS/storage/bandwidth from user-level inputs, and using estimates to drive architectural decisions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Computing precise numbers without sanity-checking, forgetting the read:write ratio, or doing the math but not using it to motivate design choices.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Convert estimates into deployment shape (number of servers, shard count, cache size), discuss peak vs average traffic (peak = 2-5x average), and acknowledge that estimates set bounds, not precision.

sections.title: Why Back-of-Envelope Matters
sections.content:
Capacity estimation isn't about being precise — it's about ruling out architecture options that obviously can't work. Whether your read QPS is 8K or 12K doesn't matter; whether it's 10K or 10M does. The right order of magnitude tells you:

- Single relational DB or sharded?
- Cache or no cache? Local L1 or distributed Redis?
- Single region or multi-region?
- Sync writes or async via queue?
- Object storage or block storage?

In an interview, the estimation step is also a way to **demonstrate that you can think in numbers** — the absence of numbers is a major red flag for a senior candidate.

sections.title: Numbers Every Engineer Should Memorize
sections.content:
**Latency (Jeff Dean's famous numbers, modernized):**

| Operation | Latency |
|---|---|
| L1 cache | 1 ns |
| L2 cache | 5 ns |
| Branch mispredict | 5 ns |
| Mutex lock/unlock | 25 ns |
| Main memory | 100 ns |
| Compress 1KB | 2 μs |
| SSD random read | 100 μs |
| Read 1MB sequentially from memory | 250 μs |
| Round trip in same datacenter | 500 μs |
| Read 1MB sequentially from SSD | 1 ms |
| HDD seek | 10 ms |
| Read 1MB sequentially from HDD | 30 ms |
| Round trip cross-continent | 100–150 ms |

**Sizes:**

| Item | Size |
|---|---|
| URL | ~50 bytes |
| Tweet / chat message | ~1 KB |
| Avatar / thumbnail | ~10 KB |
| Photo (typical) | ~100 KB |
| Document / PDF page | ~100 KB – 1 MB |
| Audio minute (compressed) | ~1 MB |
| Video minute (1080p compressed) | ~10 MB |
| 4K video minute | ~100 MB |

**Scale anchors:**

| Resource | Capacity |
|---|---|
| 1 commodity server | ~10K QPS for simple requests |
| 1 Redis instance | ~100K ops/sec |
| 1 PostgreSQL instance | ~10K writes/sec, ~50K reads/sec |
| 1 Kafka partition | ~10 MB/sec sustained |
| 1 Gbps NIC | ~125 MB/sec |
| 1 datacenter rack | ~40 servers |

sections.title: The 4 Dimensions — Always Cover All
sections.content:
**1. Traffic (QPS)**
- Daily Active Users (DAU) × actions per user ÷ 86,400 sec/day = average QPS.
- Multiply by 2–5x for peak QPS.
- Split into read QPS and write QPS using your read:write ratio (typically 10:1 to 100:1 for most consumer apps).

**2. Storage**
- Items per user × size per item × user count = total data.
- Multiply by replication factor (3x typical) for actual disk needed.
- Project growth (5 years at 2x annual = 32x).

**3. Bandwidth (network)**
- Read QPS × average response size = read bandwidth.
- Write QPS × average payload size = write bandwidth.
- Cross-region replication, CDN egress, backup bandwidth all add.

**4. Memory (cache + working set)**
- Hot working set size (top 20% of accessed data is usually 80% of traffic — Pareto).
- For caches: bytes per entry × entries × 1.3 (overhead).
- Decide if working set fits in RAM (single big instance) or needs distributed cache.

sections.title: Worked Example — Twitter-like Service
sections.content:
**Inputs:**
- 200M DAU.
- Each user posts 2 tweets/day, reads 100 tweets/day.
- Tweet = 1 KB text + 100 KB media (50% have media).

**Traffic:**
- Writes: 200M × 2 / 86,400 = ~4,600 writes/sec average; ~15K peak.
- Reads: 200M × 100 / 86,400 = ~230K reads/sec average; ~700K peak.
- Read:write ratio = ~50:1 → read-optimized architecture (cache, replicas).

**Storage (for tweets only):**
- Daily: 200M × 2 = 400M tweets/day.
- Per tweet avg = 1 KB text + 50 KB media = 51 KB.
- Daily storage = 400M × 51 KB = ~20 TB/day.
- 5 years × 365 days × 20 TB = ~36 PB.
- Replication 3x = ~110 PB on disk.

**Bandwidth:**
- Read bandwidth = 230K reads/sec × 51 KB ≈ 12 GB/sec (peak: 35 GB/sec).
- Write bandwidth = 4.6K × 51 KB ≈ 235 MB/sec (peak: 700 MB/sec).
- Cross-region replication adds ~25% → plan for ~45 GB/sec edge bandwidth at peak.

**Memory (cache):**
- Hot working set: 20% of users producing 80% of reads → cache 20% of recent tweets.
- Recent 7 days = 7 × 400M = 2.8B tweets; 20% = 560M cached.
- 1 KB metadata/tweet × 560M = 560 GB Redis cluster (sharded).

**Architectural conclusions:**
- Sharded write store (Cassandra, ~30 shards at 50K writes/sec each).
- Read tier with regional caches and CDN for media.
- Object storage (S3) for media — not relational DB.
- Multi-region active-active for read traffic; primary region for writes.

sections.title: From Estimate to Server Count
sections.content:
**Sizing rule of thumb:**

```
servers = (peak QPS × avg latency in seconds) / target utilization
```

Use Little's Law: concurrency = arrival rate × service time.

**Example:** 100K QPS, 10ms per request, target 70% utilization.
- Concurrent requests = 100K × 0.01 = 1000.
- If each server handles 100 concurrent requests → 10 servers minimum.
- Add headroom: 10 / 0.7 = ~15 servers.
- Multiply by AZ count for HA: 15 × 3 = 45 servers across 3 AZs.

**Database sizing:**
- Writes/sec / max-writes-per-instance = shard count.
- Storage / max-storage-per-instance = shard count (take the higher).
- Always round up; add 25–50% headroom for spikes and rebalancing.

**Cache sizing:**
- Hot working set in bytes / per-instance memory = cache cluster size.
- Add replicas for HA (2x or 3x).

sections.title: Peak vs Average and Time-of-Day Patterns
sections.content:
**Critical correction:** average QPS is misleading. Real systems see:

- **Diurnal peaks:** ~3x average for consumer apps, peak around 8-10pm local time.
- **Day-of-week peaks:** Sunday evening peaks for streaming; Monday morning for productivity.
- **Event spikes:** Super Bowl, election night, viral content — 10x or more.
- **Promotion / sale spikes:** Black Friday, flash sales — 50-100x for e-commerce.

**Always design for peak**, not average. A common rule:
- `peak_qps = average_qps × 3` for normal consumer apps.
- `peak_qps = average_qps × 10` for spike-prone systems.
- `peak_qps = average_qps × 100` for flash-sale systems.

**Capacity headroom:** plan for 50% utilization at peak. That gives room for:
- Failure of one AZ (33% capacity loss).
- Deployment without degradation.
- Unexpected spikes.

Auto-scaling helps but has lag (minutes); you still need baseline capacity for sudden spikes.

sections.title: Common Estimation Mistakes
sections.content:
**1. Computing average without peak.**
- 'We have 100K QPS' is meaningless without knowing if that's average or peak.

**2. Forgetting the read:write ratio.**
- A read-heavy system needs caches and replicas; a write-heavy system needs sharding and queues. Different architectures.

**3. Underestimating storage growth.**
- 1 PB today + 2x growth/year + 5-year horizon = 32 PB. Many systems get this wrong by a factor of 10.

**4. Ignoring metadata overhead.**
- A '1 KB tweet' has ~5 KB of metadata in indices, replication overhead, etc. Real on-disk footprint is 3-5x raw payload.

**5. Assuming linear scaling.**
- 10 servers handle 100K QPS does not mean 100 servers handle 1M QPS. Hot keys, lock contention, network saturation — things degrade.

**6. Not converting to architecture.**
- 'Storage = 100 PB' isn't useful unless you say 'so we need sharded object storage, not a single relational DB.'

**7. Skipping the bandwidth check.**
- 1M QPS at 100 KB each = 100 GB/sec — needs CDN; pure server-side serving is impossible at that bandwidth.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Always cover 4 dimensions:** QPS (read + write), storage, bandwidth, memory/cache.
- **Memorize the numbers:** L1=1ns, RAM=100ns, SSD=100μs, RTT in DC=500μs, cross-continent=100ms.
- **Memorize the sizes:** tweet=1KB, image=100KB, video minute=10MB.
- **Memorize the anchors:** server=10K QPS, Redis=100K ops/sec, Postgres=10K writes/sec, Kafka partition=10MB/sec.
- **Peak ≈ 3x average for consumer apps**, 10x for spike-prone, 100x for flash sales.
- **Always convert estimates to architecture decisions** — number of shards, cache size, server count, region count.
- **Use Little's Law** for server count: concurrency = arrival rate × service time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The goal**

Not precision — order-of-magnitude correctness. Whether your read QPS is 8K or 12K doesn't matter; whether it's 10K or 10M does. The right order of magnitude tells you single DB or sharded, cache or no cache, single region or global, sync or queue.

**The four dimensions, always cover all four**

1. Traffic: DAU × actions/user ÷ 86,400 = avg QPS; × 3-5 for peak; split read vs write
2. Storage: items × size × users × replication factor × growth projection
3. Bandwidth: QPS × response size = network egress; cross-region replication adds 25%
4. Memory: hot working set (Pareto: 20% of data = 80% of traffic) × 1.3 overhead

**Numbers to memorize**

Latency: L1=1ns, RAM=100ns, SSD=100μs, RTT same DC=500μs, cross-continent=100ms.

Sizes: URL=50B, tweet=1KB, image=100KB, doc=1MB, video minute=10MB.

Anchors: server=10K QPS, Redis=100K ops/sec, Postgres=10K writes/sec, Kafka partition=10MB/sec, 1Gbps=125MB/sec.

**Worked example — Twitter-like, 200M DAU, 2 tweets, 100 reads per user**

- Writes: 200M × 2 / 86,400 = 4,600/sec avg, 15K peak
- Reads: 200M × 100 / 86,400 = 230K/sec avg, 700K peak
- Read:write = 50:1 → read-optimized architecture
- Storage: 400M tweets/day × 50KB ≈ 20 TB/day; 5y × 3 replicas ≈ 110 PB
- Bandwidth: 230K reads × 50KB = 12 GB/sec read; 700 MB/sec write
- Cache: top 20% of recent tweets ≈ 560 GB Redis cluster

**Convert to architecture**

- Sharded write store (Cassandra, ~30 shards at 50K writes/sec each)
- Read tier with regional cache + CDN for media
- Object storage for media, not relational DB
- Multi-region active-active reads, primary region writes

**From estimate to server count — Little's Law**

```
servers = peak QPS × avg latency / target utilization
```

Example: 100K QPS × 10ms = 1000 concurrent. 100 per server = 10 minimum. /0.7 utilization = 15. ×3 AZs = 45 servers.

**Peak vs average — the most common mistake**

- Diurnal peaks ~3x average
- Event spikes 10x
- Flash sales 100x
- Always design for peak, capacity at 50% utilization to absorb AZ failure + deploy + spikes

**Common mistakes**

- Quoting average without peak
- Forgetting read:write ratio (drives entire architecture)
- Underestimating growth (5 years at 2x/year = 32x)
- Ignoring metadata overhead (3-5x raw payload on disk)
- Assuming linear scaling (hot keys, lock contention break it)
- Not converting numbers into architecture decisions
- Skipping bandwidth (100 GB/sec needs CDN, period)

**Recommendation**

**Always start with DAU and derive QPS/storage/bandwidth/memory in that order. Memorize the latency, size, and capacity anchors. Multiply average by 3-10x for peak. Use Little's Law to convert QPS-into-server-count. Most importantly, convert every estimate into an architectural decision — numbers without an architecture conclusion are wasted breath.**
